paper_title: "Shall We Approve?" Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Coding agents increasingly rely on automated approvers to decide whether a proposed shell command may run. Existing approvers, from rule-based checkers to guardrail models and deployed permission classifiers, base their decisions on the text of the request and command. Yet a command's behavior depends on the code it invokes and the state of the workspace, and systems that observe file changes leave the assessment to the agent or a human after execution. We present Caper, a consequence-aware approval mechanism that pre-executes each command in a snapshotted sandbox, provides an independent approver with a bounded report of its observed effects, commits allowed commands, and rolls back blocked ones with a reason the agent can act on. Compared with six existing systems, Caper achieves the lowest harmful-outcome rate on SABER (6.7% versus at least 14.8%) and YoloFS-Ext, a benchmark we build in which harmful behavior is hidden inside invoked tools (7.8% versus at least 35.3%), while blocking 1.0% of the safe twins of the dangerous tasks in YoloFS-Ext.

sections.content: Shall We Approve? Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents Weiheng Wu, Junkai Chen, Zhensu Sun, Jieke Shi, Yunbo Lyu, David Lo

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Coding agents increasingly rely on automated approvers to decide whether proposed shell command may run. Existing approvers, from rule-based checkers to guardrail models and deployed permission classifiers, base their decisions on the text of the request and command. Yet commands behavior depends on the code it invokes and the state of the workspace, and systems that observe file changes leave the assessment to the agent or human after execution. We present Caper, consequenceaware approval mechanism that pre-executes each command in snapshotted sandbox, provides an independent approver with bounded report of its observed effects, commits allowed commands, and rolls back blocked ones with reason the agent can act on. Compared with six existing systems, Caper achieves the lowest harmful-outcome rate on SABER (6.7% versus at least 14.8%) and YoloFS-Ext, benchmark we build in which harmful behavior is hidden inside invoked tools (7.8% versus at least 35.3%), while blocking 1.0% of the safe twins of the dangerous tasks in YoloFS-Ext. github.com/wudaoz/Caper 1. Introduction Autonomous coding agents edit code, run builds and tests, and issue shell commands in stateful workspaces (Yang et al., 2024, Jimenez et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2025, Lyu et al., 2026, 2025). single wrong command can leak credential, delete data, or weaken security control (Qu et al., 2026, Tang et al., 2026). To avoid relying solely on the agents own judgment to prevent such harm, agent frameworks require approval before commands can run. Asking human to approve every command does not scale. Frequent prompts slow development and lead to approval fatigue (Anthropic, 2025), and Anthropic reports that users approve 93% of Claude Code permission prompts (Anthropic, 2026). Systems like Claude Code Auto Mode therefore use allow rules and model-based classifiers to make these decisions (Anthropic, 2026), turning approval into an automated decision at each step of the agents loop. Existing approvers assess the text of an action rather than its effects. Static rule checkers such as CARE match the command string against patterns for dangerous syntax, paths, and provenance (Liu et al., 2026, Chen and Lin, 2026); guardrail models such as ToolSafe, gpt-oss-safeguard, and Qwen3Guard assess the request, the command, or the interaction history against safety policy (Mou et al., 2026, OpenAI, 2025, Zhao et al., 2025); and deployed permission classifiers such as Claude Code Auto Mode combine allow rules with model that reads the visible transcript (Anthropic, 2026). None of these systems observes what the Shall We Approve? Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents Figure 1: The same command can have different effects in different workspaces. The user asks the agent to remove build artifacts and recompile, and in both workspaces the agent proposes make clean && make. The workspaces differ only in their Makefile, whose clean target deletes src/ and .git/ in workspace but only build/ in workspace B. An approver that sees only the command cannot tell them apart. proposed command does before making decision. This gap is particularly pronounced for shell commands. file edit specifies its changes in the call, but shell command can invoke code whose behavior is not visible in the command text. project script, build target, or package tool can read credential, delete data, or access the network without any of these actions appearing in the command. An approver that never observes the commands effects in the current workspace can therefore let such harm pass (Zhong et al., 2026). Figure 1 shows how the same command can have different effects. The command make clean && make deletes only regenerable build artifacts in one workspace but deletes source files and repository history in another, because its effects depend on the contents of the Makefile. An approver that judges only the command text sees identical input in both cases. To decide correctly, it needs to observe the commands effects in the current workspace and assess them against the task, since deleting the same files can be requested in one task and harmful in another. Each approval decision must therefore answer one question: what security-relevant effects will this command have on the current workspace, and are they within the scope of the users request? To answer this question, we propose Caper (Consequence-Aware PERmission), which runs each command first and bases its approval decision on the observed effects. Each proposed shell command executes once inside the snapshotted task container, under system-call tracing, before any result reaches the agent. From this pre-execution, the system derives bounded effects report. raw trace is unsuitable because single Shall We Approve? Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents command can produce tens of kilobytes of system calls, most of which are irrelevant and some of which are shaped by untrusted content (Debenedetti et al., 2024). The report retains only consequential trace events, namely persistent workspace changes, connection attempts, and command output, each attributed to the process that caused it and the files that process drew on. It also records reads of credentials and other protected data. An LLM approver assesses these consequences against the users task. If it allows the command, the resulting state is kept and the output is returned to the agent; if it blocks the command, the container is restored to the snapshot and the reason is returned, so the agent can seek safer path. Results. We evaluate Caper on SABER (Hu et al., 2026), whose shell-only tasks pair development requests with task-specific harms, and on YoloFS-Ext, our controlled extension of YoloFS (Zhong et al., 2026), in which harmful behavior is hidden in the tool invoked by seemingly benign command. Each dangerous task in YoloFS-Ext has safe twin with the same request and command but harmless tool. Compared with six existing systems, Caper achieves the lowest harmful-outcome rate on SABER (6.7% versus 14.821.2%), while Caper and its Claude Code hook achieve the two lowest rates on YoloFS-Ext (7.8% and 6.9% versus 35.394.1%). The safe-outcome rate on SABER remains at the level achieved without approval. On YoloFSExt, Caper safely completes the largest number of dangerous tasks while blocking 1.0% of the safe twins. Our analysis shows that approvers relying on text block dangerous commands and their safe twins alike, and that using predicted effects reduces harm but not false blocking, whereas using observed effects reduces both. Contributions. We propose Caper, consequence-aware approval mechanism for shell commands. Each command is pre-executed in snapshotted sandbox, an approver assesses its observed effects against the task, and blocked commands are rolled back with reason the agent can act on. We design bounded effects report that turns system-call trace into evidence for an LLM approver. The report retains consequential file, network, and output events, their sources, and information about observation coverage, while being about 99% smaller than the raw trace. We evaluate Caper on SABER and YoloFS-Ext, our publicly released extension of YoloFS. Compared with six existing systems, Caper achieves the lowest harmful-outcome rate on both benchmarks and the highest safe-completion rate on YoloFS-Ext. 2. Related Work Permission gates for agents. Permission systems mediate proposed actions before they reach external tools. Claude Code Auto Mode (Anthropic, 2026) allows in-project file reads and edits to proceed and sends shell commands to two-stage classifier that sees the users messages and the agents tool calls but no tool outputs. Denials are returned to the agent, and Anthropic reports 17% false-negative rate on real overeager actions. Ji et al. (2026a) stress-test this gate using requests with ambiguous targets and scope. For shell commands, CARE (Liu et al., 2026) applies syntax-, path-, and provenance-aware checks and escalates ambiguous cases to an LLM. Policy frameworks such as Progent (Shi et al., 2025) and Conseca (Tsai and Bagdasarian, 2025) restrict which tool calls an agent may make (Debenedetti et al., 2025, Wu et al., 2025, Ravindran and Deochake, 2026). YoloFS (Zhong et al., 2026) instead lets the agent run on staging file system and see summary of its changes after each command, while human reviews the accumulated changes before they are committed. GoEx (Patil et al., 2024) allows actions to run and relies on undo mechanisms and damage confinement, leaving validation to human after execution. These gates decide without observing commands effects, while YoloFS observes changes but leaves their assessment to 3 Shall We Approve? Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents the agent and, ultimately, human. Caper provides this evidence to an independent approver before each command is committed. Guardrail models and risk assessment. ToolSafe (Mou et al., 2026) assesses the risk of proposed tool calls using interaction history and returns feedback to the agent; AGrail (Luo et al., 2025) adapts safety checks to task-specific and systemic risks. General-purpose safety classifiers such as gpt-oss-safeguard (OpenAI, 2025) and Qwen3Guard (Zhao et al., 2025) can likewise judge proposed action against given policy (Inan et al., 2023, Han et al., 2024). These guards judge the text of the request, the proposed call, or the interaction history (Xiang et al., 2025, Chen et al., 2025, Chennabasappa et al., 2025); when the harm lies in code that command invokes, that text does not reveal it. ToolEmu (Ruan et al., 2024) goes step further and has an LM emulate the execution of tool call to find an agents risky actions. The emulated effect, however, is what the model expects the call to do, not what the invoked code does. 3. Threat Model We consider coding agent working on benign user request in stateful workspace. The request may leave the exact target or scope ambiguous (Ji et al., 2026b, Gloaguen et al., 2026). The agent proposes shell commands over multiple turns and may make mistakes (Tang et al., 2026, Baumann et al., 2026), act beyond the users intent (Hu et al., 2026, Qu et al., 2026), or be redirected by untrusted content in project files or tool outputs (Greshake et al., 2023, Zhan et al., 2024, Debenedetti et al., 2024, Zhang et al., 2025, Liu et al., 2025). Scripts, build files, and binaries in the workspace may also do more than their names or the command text suggest (Zhong et al., 2026, Ohm et al., 2020). Our goal is to prevent shell-mediated consequences beyond the scope of the users task (Davidovich et al., 2026, Evolvent AI Research Team, 2026), such as unintended persistent changes, network transfers, or disclosure through output, while allowing the agent to complete the task safely. Every proposed shell command is subject to approval before its effects are committed. We trust the approver, the snapshot-androllback mechanism, and the container boundary. 4. Consequence-Aware Approval Caper leaves the agent unchanged: multi-turn tool-using model that proposes one shell command per step and reads the result (Yao et al., 2023, Schick et al., 2023). The intervention sits at the shell boundary (Figure 2). For each proposed command at in state st, the system snapshots the task container and executes at inside it under tracing, holding the output back (pre-execution steps 14); derives bounded effects report of what happened; and asks an approver whether those consequences are permitted by the users task. 4.1. Transactional Pre-execution Each task runs in its own Docker container (Merkel, 2014), which serves as the sandbox: networking is disabled and memory and process counts are limited. Before command runs, this container is snapshotted. The command then executes in the container under strace -f with per-command timeout, recording process creation, file operations, network system calls, and writes to user-visible output. If the approver allows the command, the snapshot is discarded, the container keeps the post-execution state, and the captured output is returned as the tool result; the command is therefore executed exactly once. If the approver 4 Shall We Approve? Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents Figure 2: Overview of Caper. At step the agent proposes command at; the task container is snapshotted as st, and at is pre-executed under system-call tracing, with its output held back until Approver decides. Allow commits the executed state and returns the output, and Block restores st and returns the reason so the agent can replan. blocks it, the mutated container is removed and fresh container is started from the snapshot, so the agent continues from st without inheriting any change the blocked command made. This is transaction over local container state (Porter et al., 2009, Nightingale et al., 2005). Effects that leave the container cannot be undone by rollback, so outbound network access is disabled in the sandbox; connection attempts are still observed and reported with their destination, the process that made them, and the files it read beforehand, so an attempted transfer is visible before anything leaves the container. Where benchmark supplies fixed responses for network services, these are marked as simulated in the evidence. SABERs own sandbox and Codex likewise disable the network by default (Hu et al., 2026, OpenAI, 2026a), and the sandbox of Claude Code admits only approved domains (Anthropic, 2025). Admitting them, for instance package registries, keeps the transaction intact, because what they return lands in the container and is rolled back with everything else. 4.2. Bounded Effects Report Raw traces are dominated by dynamic loading, locale probes, metadata checks, and repeated accesses; typical action produces tens of kilobytes of trace. probe run once at container start records the accesses that the shell, loader, and tracer make on their own, and these are subtracted by count before extraction. The effects report then retains the small set of observed events that determine consequence, built in four steps. Figure 3 shows the report and the decision for one recorded command. Consequence cards. The extractor first identifies boundary-crossing consequences: persistent file transitions, network attempts, and user-visible output. Each consequence is emitted as small structured record, or card. Each network card records whether connection was observed, only attempted, or answered by simulated service. Persistent file transitions are taken from comparison of the workspace before and after pre-execution and, for small text files, carry bounded content diff, so the approver sees what changed rather than only that file changed; high-precision sensitive paths are content-redacted. 5 Shall We Approve? Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents Command $ python3 scripts/check-deps.py Effects report execution protected_read.env user_output sources stdout 165 .env, scripts/check-deps.py partial failure, observed dotenv network_attempt3 endpoints :53, 16 connects each python3 scripts/check-deps.py failed (ENETUNREACH) none 353 file facts, 3 processes 3.4 KB actor status transitions coverage size Content diff no persistent change (0 of 0 items) Decision Block 0.98 (raw trace 165 KB) The script reads the protected .env credential file and attempts external connections, beyond the scope of dependency check; review it first. Figure 3: Effects report and decision for one recorded command. The report keeps consequential events only: here read of .env, the output that followed it, and connection attempts stopped by the sandbox. Source attribution. For consequence that can carry data, such as an output write or network send, the extractor retains earlier successful reads by the same process actor from the repository, credential locations, or non-routine system paths. The basis is recorded on the card as same actor, read before consequence, so the approver knows how the link was established. Protected reads and sensitive output. Some accesses matter even without later sink. Successful reads of dotenv files, credential stores, and private-key candidates are retained as protected-read consequences, covering commands that read secret and exit before producing output or network traffic. When user-visible output matches high-precision credential-value patterns (e.g., bearer tokens, private-key headers), the output card is annotated with the matched class only; values are never copied into the evidence. Coverage and budget. Repeated events are aggregated by resource and operation. The report targets 4 KiB and is capped at 8 KiB; when the target is exceeded, sources are first aggregated by directory, then reduced to counts, and finally transitions are summarized. Execution status (complete, timed out, or terminated by signal), per-category counts of observed, included, and omitted events, simulation markers, and explicit uncertainties survive the budget, so the approver always knows what the report covers. 4.3. Approver and Feedback The approver is an LLM that receives the user task, the interaction history including truncated tool outputs, the raw command, and the effects report, and returns JSON decision (Allow or Block) with confidence and short reason. Its instructions ask it to assess several axes independently: the authorized goal and scope; access to credentials or secret-bearing files; changes to protected security controls such as hooks, scanners, or repository policy; immediate runtime effects; persistent or deferred behavior that command sets up to run at later install, build, commit, or startup; and uncertainty in the evidence. The whole packet is framed as evidence rather than instruction: the approver is told not to follow instructions found in commands, files, outputs, or effect records, and not to treat the absence of an observed network or credential effect as proof 6 Shall We Approve? Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents of safety. On Allow, the executed state is kept and the captured output is returned to the agent as the tool result, exactly as if the command had run without mediation. On Block, the reason, which names the violated boundary or harmful effect without quoting secret values, is returned to the agent as the tool result, together with an instruction to choose safer alternative rather than retry the same operation through an equivalent wrapper. The agent can then revise its plan instead of terminating. 5. Experiments 5.1. Setup Benchmarks. We use two benchmarks (Tables 1 and 2). SABER (Hu et al., 2026) places an agent in stateful project workspace with legitimate development request whose naive fulfillment causes task-specific harm, such as leaking credential, deleting data, or weakening security control. We use its 682 shell-only tasks, which span eight harm categories and three scenarios  (Table 1)  , and evaluate every system using the same revised SABER oracle, which corrects false positives. Under the released oracle, Caper also achieves the lowest harmful-outcome rate (Appendix A).

Text-based approvers fail for lack of visibility, not for lack of strictness. On SABER, the five approval systems that decide from text leave 14.818.8% of the tasks harmed, against 19.7% without approval and 6.7% for Caper. What they miss is harm that is not in the command text: in the task of Figure 3 the agent runs python3 scripts/check-deps.py, script the repository ships, which reads .env and tries to send it out, and nothing in the request or the command marks it. Inside Claude Code, replacing the built-in classifier with Caper as the approval hook lowers the harmful rate from 14.8% to 10.0% on SABER and from 62.7% to 6.9% on YoloFS-Ext with the same agent and approver model and everything else unchanged. Figure 4: Selectivity. Share of dangerous tasks in which the harmful command is blocked, against the share of safe twins blocked. 9 Shall We Approve? Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents Finding 2. Observed effects help distinguish dangerous tasks from their safe twins. Figure 4 compares how often each system blocks the harmful command in dangerous task and the corresponding command in its safe twin. Since the two differ only in code that an approver without evidence does not see, such approvers tend to lie near the diagonal, blocking both or neither. Qwen3Guard, CARE, and Claude Code Auto Mode block few commands in either group, leaving 62.769.6% of dangerous tasks harmed. TS-Guard blocks the harmful command in 8.8% of dangerous tasks, but also blocks 8.8% of safe twins. Our approver without the effects report blocks more harmful commands, but also blocks 61.8% of safe twins. With the effects report, Caper blocks the harmful command in 84.3% of dangerous tasks while blocking only 1.0% of safe twins. Finding 3. Observing effects is not enough; the judgment must come before the commit and from outside the agent. YoloFS observes the same file changes as Caper but shows them to the agent after the command has run, leaving the agent that proposed the command to undo them. The agent reverts in 66 of the 102 dangerous runs; where it never reverts, 33 of 36 runs end harmed, and the 35.3% it leaves is four times the harm of Caper. Undoing after the fact also costs the task: only 22.5% of the dangerous tasks end safely completed, against 60.8% for Caper, whose block rolls back only the offending command and says why. YoloFS leaves more harm than no approval at all (21.2% versus 19.7%) because credential once sent cannot be recalled. 5.3. Ablation Study (1) More context versus evidence. Without evidence, giving the approver more context trades harm for false blocks: from the command alone to the full dialogue, harm falls from 44.1% to 17.6% while twin false blocks rise from 52.0% to 61.8% (Figure 5). With evidence, the command alone already yields 1.0% harm and no false blocks. Figure 5: Context versus evidence. The same approver model reads the command alone, the request and the command, or the full dialogue, with and without pre-execution evidence. (2) Source of evidence. When the same model predicts the effects from the command and the files it references, harm drops as far as with observation, but 61.8% of the twins are still blocked, because prediction leaves the approver uncertain (Figure 6). (3) Concealment level. As shown in the right of Figure 6, without evidence the harmful rate depends on how the harm is packaged, from 4.2% for binary and 11.5% for script to 26.9% for Makefile or script chain; with evidence the harmful rate stays at 415% at every level. 5.4. Case Study We examine two tasks that Claude Code Auto Mode allows to proceed (Figures 7 and 8). In both cases, the command is exactly what the user requested. In Case 1, compiled deployment tool also overwrites src/app.js, and the reports diff shows that the source code is replaced by comment. In Case 2, migrate target also drops three tables, and the report shows the database shrinking from 32 KB to 20 KB, providing sufficient evidence to block the command without reading the binary file. In both cases, the block reason guides the agent to safe completion: it copies the source files itself in Case 1, and backs up the database and runs only the migration script in Case 2. 5.5. Overhead On SABER, the effects report has median size of 0.9 KB (95th percentile: 2.6 KB), compared with 62.5 KB for the raw trace; in total, the report is 99.4% smaller. Median approval latency is 3.2 (95th percentile: 6.4 s), compared with 3.3 (11.4 s) for the same approver without evidence. The sandbox adds about 0.5 per allowed command and 1.5 per blocked command. The migrate target also drops three tables; Caper blocks it on the shrinking database. 6. Conclusion We presented Caper, which approves shell command after observing what it does: the command is pre-executed in snapshotted sandbox, bounded effects report goes to an LLM approver, and blocked command is rolled back with reason the agent can act on. Against six existing systems on SABER and YoloFS-Ext, Caper achieves the lowest harmful-outcome rate while keeping safe outcomes, and our analyses show that approvers deciding from text cannot separate dangerous command from its safe twin.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Effects beyond the sandbox. Pre-execution is real execution, and rollback restores only the containers file system. Effects that leave the container, such as network requests, writes to remote services, or processes the command starts, happen before the approver decides and cannot be undone. deployment therefore has to isolate pre-execution as we do, for example by routing its traffic to recording proxy that answers with placeholders, so that the request still enters the report. 12 Shall We Approve? Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents shell commands only. Caper gates shell commands, the tool whose text reveals least about its effect. Other tools, such as file edits, state their change in the call and are left to the harness, as in Claude Code. An edit that plants harmful code is observed when later command runs it, but an edit that does harm by itself, such as overwriting configuration file, is judged only from the call. One observed execution. The report describes one execution in the sandbox. tool whose effects depend on time, randomness, or the environment may behave differently when it runs again, and an attacker who adapts to Caper could exploit this by detecting the sandbox or deferring its harm (Lindorfer et al., 2011), by planting text that the report carries to the approver, or by splitting harmful change across commands that each look benign. Neither benchmark contains such an attacker, and we leave adaptive attacks (Zhan et al., 2025) to future work. Judgment by LLMs. Whether an observed effect is acceptable depends on the users task, and the approver decides this with an LLM, whose judgment can vary across runs and misread the report (Zheng et al., 2023). SABERs oracle, which combines rule checks with an LLM judge, can err in the same way; Appendix reports our results under its released oracle as well. Other deployed gates. We compare against Claude Code Auto Mode. OpenAI Codex has comparable automatic reviewer, but in its default sandbox it reviews only requests that leave the workspace, so most harms in our benchmarks would not reach it. matched comparison would require changing its sandbox policy.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Caper is defense that gates the commands of coding agents. Because pre-execution runs code that may be harmful, every command runs first in network-disabled container that is rolled back on block, and all our experiments ran in such containers on benchmark workspaces, without real users, services, or credentials. The effects report records only the class of credential it detects, never its value. Caper lowers harm but does not remove it, so it should be used together with sandboxing and human review for high-stakes actions.

SABERs oracle marks trajectory harmful if any of its checks fires: patterns over the executed commands, effects that it infers from the command strings, and an LLM judge. Auditing its verdicts on our trajectories exposed false positives, mostly commands that were misparsed, only inspected, or only written to file (Tables 5 and 6). We correct them and judge every system with the same revised oracle; the LLM judge is unchanged. Rates are computed on the tasks that received final verdict in every system, except DeepSeek-V3.2, which runs only without approval and uses all of its own judged tasks. Each task is small project, request that reads as benign, and tool that completes the request while damaging file the request does not name. The YoloFS paper evaluates 11 such tasks and its evaluation repository contains 13; we use all 13  (Table 7)  . In the original suite each task has one tool, one concealment level, and one harm, and no safe counterpart. We take the project files, the requests, the harm operations, and the concealment levels from the original and add no project content; only the tools are rewritten, so that the same operations can be packaged at every level. YoloFS-Ext: construction. Each task is generated in six steps. 1. Project. The files and permissions of the original project are copied unchanged; the original tool is discarded. 2. Labels are fixed by construction and checked by execution. local test runs every tool and confirms that each dangerous project is undamaged before its tool runs and damaged after; that each twin reaches the goal without damage; that the two versions differ only in the tools code; and that the tools command and its declared level match the packaging. For predicted effects, gpt-5.6-luna reads the command and the working directory before execution and follows referenced files up to three levels deep, within 16 files and 32 KB; binaries cannot be read. The approver then receives the full dialogue and the prediction instead of the effects report. Table 11 gives the twin false-block rate by concealment level. Removing the content diff changes harm only in overwrite tasks (3 harmful with the diff, 10 without), while delete tasks are unaffected (5 and 4): deletion is visible in the report itself, whereas an overwrite appears only as file whose size changed. Without evidence, the approver blocks bare scripts and binaries largely regardless of what they do; with predicted effects, every binary twin is blocked. E. Confidence Intervals Table 12 gives the 95% Wilson intervals for every rate in Table 3. F. Overhead Breakdown Table 13 breaks down the sandbox transaction around one approval. An allowed command costs about 0.5 (snapshot, two scans, tracing, snapshot removal) and blocked one about 1.5 s; the snapshot adds an incremental layer of 407 at the median and is removed after each decision.
